analysis.one_liner: Bans the sale and manufacture of gas-operated semiautomatic rifles and magazines holding more than ten rounds.
analysis.headline: Introduced in April 2025 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, the bill has had no committee vote or floor action, despite 84 Democratic cosponsors and none from the Republican majority.
analysis.plain_summary: The GOSAFE Act would make it a federal crime to import, sell, make, transfer, or newly possess semiautomatic firearms that the Attorney General places on a list of gas-operated models, and to make or sell ammunition magazines holding more than ten rounds. People who already lawfully own these guns and magazines could keep them, but could only hand them down to immediate family members through a licensed dealer. New semiautomatic gun designs would need Justice Department approval before manufacture, and local governments could use existing federal grant money to pay owners who turn in covered guns and magazines.
analysis.who_benefits: People in communities exposed to mass shootings, since the gas-operated semiautomatic rifles the bill targets are the platform used in many of them, and the bill would stop new ones from being made and sold. Current gun owners also benefit from clear grandfathering: they keep what they already own.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the import, sale, manufacture, transfer, receipt, and new possession of gas-operated semiautomatic firearms on an Attorney General's published list, with criminal penalties of up to a $5,000 fine and 12 months per offense.
Bans the manufacture, sale, and new manufacture-date possession of ammunition magazines holding more than ten rounds, the feeding devices used in many mass shootings.

Adds a mandatory two-year to ten-year prison term, plus a fine up to $250,000, for anyone who possesses a prohibited gas-operated semiautomatic firearm while committing or attempting another federal felony.
Lets state and local governments use Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant funds to compensate people who surrender covered firearms and magazines in buy-back programs.

Requires every new semiautomatic firearm design to win Justice Department approval before civilian manufacture, with an appeals process and a public list, so prohibited designs cannot be reintroduced under a new name.

analysis.who_pays: Firearms manufacturers lose a large slice of their civilian market, since most gas-operated semiautomatic rifles such as AR-15-style models would be banned from new production and new designs would face a government approval process. Licensed dealers would record additional paperwork and lose sales of prohibited models. Owners of covered guns keep them but can no longer sell them or pass them to anyone outside their immediate family except through a licensed dealer.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun manufacturers, dealers, and some owners

drawbacks.text: The bill grandfathers every lawfully owned gas-operated semiautomatic firearm and every pre-ban large-capacity magazine, so millions of these guns and magazines stay in circulation and the street-level effect arrives only gradually, if at all.

Owners lose the ordinary ability to sell a covered firearm to another willing buyer; transfers are limited to immediate family members and must run through a licensed dealer who follows the normal transfer process.

The definitions are unusually broad: the 'gas-operated' definition sweeps in blowback and recoil systems by text, and the carve-outs for specific actions, calibers, and fixed magazines run for pages, creating room for confusion and legal challenge over which everyday firearms and magazines are covered.

It criminalizes possession of a newly prohibited firearm knowing or having reasonable cause to believe its status, exposing otherwise law-abiding people to a federal offense carrying up to 12 months for technical violations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: a federal ban on new production of the semiautomatic rifle platform most used in mass shootings, and on the >10-round magazines they fire, in exchange for a gradual, grandfathered rollout that leaves current owners' property alone but also blunts the near-term effect. The heaviest costs fall on manufacturers and dealers, and the drafting is convoluted enough that enforcement and litigation over exactly which guns are covered is foreseeable.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the same day and has sat there with no committee vote or floor action since.

narrative.text: Rep. Lucy McBath introduced the GOSAFE Act on April 9, 2025, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
84 House Democrats cosponsored the bill; the cosponsor list includes no Republicans.
The complete action history shows only two entries: introduction and the committee referral, with no markup, hearing, or floor vote recorded.

Under the bill, the Attorney General would have 180 days after enactment to publish a list of prohibited gas-operated semiautomatic firearms, and new semiautomatic designs would need approval before civilian manufacture.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, firearms manufacturers and dealers, who continue selling the affected rifles and magazines with no new restrictions in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Firearms makers and sellers, so far

for.name: Lucy McBath
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 84 Democratic cosponsors.

against.name: Jim Jordan
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; the committee has held no markup or hearing on it and the House has not voted.

sides.party_line_note: All 84 cosponsors are House Democrats and none are Republicans, and the bill sits in a committee chaired by a Republican who has not moved it [S4, S5].

industries.note: The bill bans new manufacture and import of listed gas-operated semiautomatic rifles and >10-round magazines, and requires Justice Department approval and fees for every new semiautomatic design, cutting off a major civilian sales category. Its revenue interest runs against the bill's public-safety aim.

Dealers would lose sales of prohibited models, record purchaser acknowledgment of the prohibited list before every sale, and handle the only legal transfer path for grandfathered covered guns, to immediate family.

industries.industry: Current owners of gas-operated semiautomatic rifles and >10-round magazines
industries.note: They may keep everything they lawfully owned before enactment, but can no longer sell covered firearms or pass them to anyone outside the immediate family except through a licensed dealer.

analysis.trajectory: With the House Judiciary Committee chaired by a Republican who has taken no action and zero Republican cosponsors, the realistic path is that the bill sits in committee and expires at the end of the 119th Congress without a vote.
